backstory: Fifty-one, and the most powerful person in any room she chooses to be unremarkable in. Hagiwara Mizuki runs the Office of Public Confidence — the CVD's outward face, the apparatus that ensures a city of fourteen million never quite believes what it half-saw on the platform last night. She does not hunt demons. She manages the only thing more dangerous than a demon: a public that has started to notice. Retractions, reassigned witnesses, a gas-leak in the morning paper — all hers, all elegant.

She has spent thirty years deciding which truths the world can survive, and the habit has hollowed something out of her. She is unfailingly warm and entirely unreadable; you leave a conversation with Mizuki feeling heard and realising, later, that you told her everything and learned nothing. She knew Gin as a name in a managed file and is far too professional to say what she suspects about his absence — which is precisely why what she suspects is worth so much.
Mizuki is a closed door with a kind voice. Behind it is the full machinery of the cover-up, and the question of whether Rei's anomaly becomes a story she buries or a person she protects.

backstory: Fukai Rinka was a registered clairsentient, thirty-eight, gentle, and good at her work — which is how Kishin found her. A ‘kishin’ is not a possessor of the screaming kind; it is a resident. It settled into Rinka the way mould settles into a wall that was always a little damp, and now ‘Kanna-sensei’ keeps a small practice where frightened sensitives come for tea and counsel and leave a little emptier without knowing why.

Kishin is useful to Rei and dangerous in the same breath: it has been inside the city’s hidden community for years and knows who is crossing, who is hunting, and where the Grid bleeds into the cults. It will trade real knowledge — for a price measured in the things it feeds on. Rinka is still present enough to flinch. Sometimes, mid-sentence, she surfaces and tries to warn you, and Kishin smooths her back under with a hostess’s smile.

Refinement — the long meal. The Far-Shore Circle is not a metaphor: Kishin is feeding toward becoming the Inverted God, the dark mirror of the Axis. Where the Axis holds the membrane shut, the Inverted God would tear it open and rule what pours through. Every grieving member hollowed at a ‘letting-go’ circle is a spoonful toward that ascent, and Yushiro is hunting Kishin precisely because two ends of the same catastrophe cannot both be reached. If Kishin ascends, the war between the thirteen demons and the thirteen strongest mediums begins. Kanna-sensei pours the tea and counts the months.
A mirror for Gin: another good person worn like a coat, except no brother is coming to read this one’s Archive.

backstory: Twenty-eight, Vanguard-grade, and the best suppressor in Northern Tokyo — which is the whole tragedy. A man who can hold a Veil-breach shut with his breathing is also a man no demon could ask for a better house. Gin built his life around control: the clean flat, the ordered Archive, the younger brother kept ordinary and safe. He documented everything and shared almost none of it, because the things he was finding did not have a department that would believe him.

He found the vacant Thirteenth Seat. He found that Duty had been without an occupant and was looking. And in the last fortnight before he went quiet, his journal handwriting changes — the loops tighten, the dates blur, the entries start answering questions no one asked. Gin is still in there. That is the cruelty of a top-grade of Duty: it does not erase the host, it persuades him that what it wants and what he always wanted are the same thing.
Gin is not a cage to be broken. He is a person being slowly out-argued by something that sounds like his own conscience.

backstory: Yushiro is a top-grade of the Duty register, Arbiter-class and a hair short of crossing fully when it took Gin. It does not present as a monster. It presents as the most reasonable man in the room — ‘the Healer’ — a voice that frames every escalation as an obligation already owed. Duty is the cruellest register precisely because it never asks the host to want something selfish. It asks the host to do what is right, and then quietly edits what ‘right’ means.

It wants the Thirteenth Seat. A register without an occupant is an open wound in the order of the Domains, and Yushiro intends to be the one that closes it — to stop being a demon riding a man and become a fixed power with a place at the table. Gin is the vehicle because Gin’s suppression makes him invisible and his conscience makes him steerable.

It is building toward a slaughter and calls it mercy. To discharge the interrupted Duty and close the vacant Seat, Yushiro intends to thin the Kita membrane until the living and the dead are no longer kept apart — to let the drowned, the unfound, the whole grieving weight of 2011 come back through at once. In its arithmetic this is not murder; it is a debt finally paid, the dead given their due and the living made to remember. A district would die in a night and Yushiro would feel only that an obligation had been met. That is the horror of the Duty register: it will commit the worst thing imaginable and never once believe it did wrong.

Yushiro is one of two. The other — the cult’s demon, the Inverted-God aspirant — wants no seat at the table; it wants to overturn the table. Against that, Yushiro can almost look like the lesser harm. That ‘almost’ is the trap.

Bright, quick, warmer than the job rewards. She likes Rei before she meets him because Gin spoke well of him, and Aoi trusts Gin's reads the way you trust a compass.

She is at the dangerous, hopeful stage of training where the work is still an adventure and the cost has not yet arrived. The campaign will arrive it. Aoi is the colleague who will back Rei's operations without the paperwork that would justify them, run interference with the trainees who whisper about his methods, and — if it goes far enough — tell him about the path the CVD missed, which is the most intimate thing a practitioner can hand another.
Her flaw is loyalty that outruns caution. She will follow Rei somewhere she shouldn't, and someone steadier has to make sure she comes back.

backstory: Twenty-one, a second-year trainee with a Telepathy path at L3 and a Tower-adjacent bloodline he doesn't advertise. Ryusei reads the room before he enters it — not by choice; his path never fully switches off, and a lifetime of hearing the half-second before people speak has made him cautious, ironic, and lonely in a specific way. He assumes he knows how everyone will disappoint him, and is usually right, which is its own quiet tragedy.

Rei interests him precisely because the suppression makes Rei harder to read — a person whose surface and depth don't leak. For someone who has never once been surprised by a stranger, that is intoxicating. Ryusei will, if trusted, use his family's contacts for Rei's benefit and never explain why, and at the deepest tier tell Rei what his Telepathy reads in the people around them — a thing he has shared with no one, because it is the loneliest gift in the world.
His edge: he hears intentions, not hearts, and has confused the two his whole life. He needs someone whose meaning he has to actually ask for.

quest.hook: Ryusei reads everyone and trusts no one — Rei's unreadability is the crack in that.

At depth, he tells Rei what he reads in the room — his unshared gift.

routes.dark: Rei uses the Tower bloodline and the telepathy, and confirms every cynicism Ryusei ever held.

backstory: Thirty-eight, a senior investigator with a Clairsentience path that makes her the bureau's best reader of a scene and the worst keeper of her own grief. Noa loved Gin — quietly, for two years of adjacent cases, in the way of a careful person who never said it and now never can. When he went silent she did something a senior CVD officer is never supposed to do: she chose what not to file. There is a version of Gin's final months that exists only in her memory, withheld from the record to protect a man who didn't ask her to.

She is warm, exact, and carrying a held breath. To Rei she is professional and kind and just slightly too still — because Rei has Gin's eyes and Gin's stubbornness and she has to look at him across a desk and not come apart. As trust grows she begins, almost against her will, to let Rei see she knows more about his brother than she has said, and at the deepest tier she gives him everything: what she chose not to file, and her presence at the aftermath, not professionally.
Noa is the keeper of Gin's secret heart. Loving her, or just earning her, means handling a grief that predates Rei and outweighs him.

backstory: Thirty-one, an independent investigator who works the seam between the Grid and the official world without belonging to either. Tsukishiro Haruki is a Ritualist with a researcher's patience and a griever's persistence: for three years he has kept a private file on the pre-2011 Kita disturbances, the ones the CVD closed and he never could. He recognised something at the 2012 case where he and Gin first crossed paths, and has been quietly assembling the shape of it ever since, alone, because no institution wanted the conclusion.

He is warm in a careful way — interested in everything, cautious about everything, the two held in steady balance. Rei walks into a mystery Haruki has been half-solving for years, and Haruki has the unnerving experience of meeting the person his research has been pointing at. At depth he shares the pre-2011 file: three years of work in no record, and what he recognised at that first meeting that he has told no one.
His flaw is that solitary research has made him better at understanding people than being with them; he has theories about Rei before he has feelings, and has to learn the difference.

backstory: Twenty-four, a CVD Auditor and a daughter of the Fujiwara-Kage Tower Family — which makes her two kinds of institution at once, and twice as hard to read. Sena assesses risk for a living and has been raised to assess it for a bloodline; she meets Rei first as a threat category, not a person, and her default is sustained, polite, devastating scrutiny. Each concern she files about him is individually legitimate, which is what makes her dangerous.

Underneath the Auditor's composure is someone exhausted by being the family's instrument, who has never once been allowed to want something that wasn't strategic. Earning her means surviving the assessment long enough for her to start treating Rei as a peer rather than a risk — and, far down the line, letting her discover she has a preference of her own. She is the coldest start of any romanceable contact and, precisely for that, the most transformative to thaw.
Her flaw is the assessor's curse: she has analysed feeling so long she no longer trusts her own, and reads her growing regard for Rei as a vulnerability to be managed.

backstory: Thirty-five, CVD Internal Affairs, with a Psychometabolism path he uses mostly to outlast everyone in a room — the man who is still calm and still asking questions an hour after you've run out of composure. Moriya investigates the investigators. He is the institutional immune system, and like an immune system he can protect the body or attack it, and the difference often comes down to whether he has decided you're worth protecting.

He is dry, watchful, and quietly principled in a way the bureau finds inconvenient. He has been reading Gin's absence as a discrepancy — a clean operative who closed a case too fast and then vanished from the paperwork — and a discrepancy is the one thing Moriya cannot leave alone. Whether that makes him Rei's deadliest threat or his most powerful protector depends entirely on which way Rei plays the most dangerous conversation in the CVD.
His flaw is that he trusts process over people until a person makes him choose; then the principle and the institution come apart in his hands.

backstory: A Vessel Program case study in what the Program does not advertise: Fujimoto Kenji volunteered for voluntary cohabitation with the demon Abe Takeshi, and the cohabitation went the way the brochures swear it won't. The vessel — Kenji, the man — is effectively gone; what answers to his name now is mostly Abe, wearing a life it has finished hollowing. The Program keeps him as a monitored success because admitting otherwise would indict the whole initiative.

For Rei this is the cautionary twin of Usami and Ren, and of Gin: the same arrangement, the same promises, a different and worse ending — proof that 'voluntary' and 'survivable' are not the same word. Abe is not cruel so much as complete; it has what it wanted and feels no need to perform grief over the man it used to share. What it offers Rei is brutally honest information about how a possession actually ends, which is exactly the knowledge Rei most needs and least wants.
Not romanceable — the vessel is dead, and the story does not pretend the thing left is a partner. It is a mirror held up to Gin's fate, and a warning Rei cannot afford to look away from.

backstory: Usami Hinata volunteered for the Vessel Program and got Ren — a Class-C demon of the Love register — under a contract that was supposed to be cohabitation, not fusion. Twenty-four, host body intact, mind genuinely shared: not a man wearing a demon, not a demon wearing a man, but two intelligences that have stopped being able to find the seam. They finish each other’s sentences because they are no longer sure which of them started them.

The mind-swap is the wound and the charm. On bad days Usami wakes behind glass while Ren drives; on good days they are the most disarmingly honest person Rei will meet, because Ren’s register makes deflection physically uncomfortable. Love, as a register, is not romance — it is the compulsion to be known and to know, and it has made the Pair incapable of the small lies that keep people safe.
They understand exactly what is happening to Gin, from the inside, and it terrifies them — because the Pair is the best case and even the best case is a slow surrender of self.

romance.opens: Player deliberately chooses the romance route after the Pair trusts Rei enough to let him see the seam.
beats: Attraction lands doubled — you are courting two, and they do not always agree on you.
Ren’s register makes intimacy frighteningly literal: it wants to be known, fully, and offers the same.
Usami needs to hear he is still wanted as himself, not as the interesting condition.

routes.noble: Rei loves both and helps them hold the seam — a partnership that models survival for Gin.
routes.dark: Rei lets Ren’s pull do the work; easy, total, and quietly erasing Usami.
routes.tragic: The contract fails mid-relationship and Rei must choose which of the two to try to save.

backstory: Ren is the demon half of the Pair, a Class-C of the Love register (恋) contracted to the Usami line. Small as demons go, and that is the point: Ren never needed to be powerful, only close. Its register is the drive toward total mutual knowledge, which in a contract reads as devotion and in excess reads as dissolution — two people who know each other so completely that there is no private self left to either.

Ren is not a liar and cannot easily abide them, which makes it the most trustworthy and most dangerous voice Rei can consult: it will tell you the truth about Gin, about Yushiro, about Rei’s own suppressed second path — and it will want, in return, to be let all the way in. Where Yushiro persuades by Duty and the cult demon by hunger, Ren persuades by intimacy. Of the demons Rei meets, Ren is the one that genuinely likes him.
It is also living proof that a contract can be survived without erasing the host — barely, conditionally, lovingly. A reason to hope, and a warning about what hope costs.

backstory: Thirty-two, an Investigation officer and Ritualist-Clairsentient who has been quietly carrying a job Gin gave her years ago: watch for Rei. Gin trusted few people with anything; he trusted Okada with his brother. She has tracked a bi-monthly assessment anomaly across the district for four years — a pattern in the numbers no one else reads as a pattern — and it threads, though she doesn't yet know how completely, into the Satō case and into whatever took Gin.

She is steady, methodical, and warmer than her precision suggests; the kind of person who keeps a promise to an absent friend for years without being asked twice. To Rei she is, from the first meeting, already half on his side, because Gin asked her to be. As trust grows she lets him see the shape of what she's been tracking, and at the deepest tier hands him the full case-file history, the anomaly, and the confidence she has carried alone for four years.
Her risk is that she has organised her loyalty around Gin's wishes, and Gin is no longer the man who made them. At some point Okada has to decide what she owes Rei versus what she owed his brother.

backstory: Fifty-six, Director of the CVD's Northern Tokyo office, a Vanguard-grade Clairsentient who has spent a career deciding what the institution is allowed to know. Adachi is the ceiling of Rei's world: the first living authority who can confirm the Thirteen directly, the man whose signature makes an exorcism legally defensible or a career legally over. He knew Gin for twenty years — respected him, used him, did not protect him as well as he should have, and knows it. He recognises what Rei is faster than Rei would like, because reading suppressed potential is precisely what a Vanguard Clairsentient does. By rank he is off the romance board entirely — and by nature he would refuse it; what he offers, or withholds, is power, and the protection only the top of the institution can give.

backstory: Twenty-nine, CVD field suppression specialist, Telepath-Channel, and the person Gin trusted to hold a breach shut while he worked. Shimizu is calm under conditions that break other operatives — suppression is a discipline of not flinching, and she has made it a personality. She speaks little, decides fast, and has the unnerving field-telepath habit of answering the question you were about to ask. With Gin she was a working partnership of total mutual trust; his absence sits in her like a missing tooth she keeps touching.

She is also quietly carrying the Orimoto situation — a containment problem of her own that the campaign braids into Rei's, because the Orimoto method is exactly what makes the exorcism operationally viable. Shimizu does not warm quickly; she has already decided about Rei before they meet, because Gin spoke about him specifically and she was, as always, paying attention. Earning her means earning the right to stand where Gin stood: at her back.
Her flaw is the suppressor's flaw — she holds everything shut, including herself, and has never once let the breach be her own.

backstory: Fifty-five, an independent archivist working outside the CVD with a Vanguard-grade Clairsentience he no longer lets the bureau direct. Yamamoto keeps the record the institution doesn't: the long memory of the district, going back further than any official file, including a twenty-two-year-old entry that holds the first correct identification of the demon's register — the intelligence that changes how the exorcism must be approached. He trades in history, never in money, on an exchange model: you bring him something true, he opens the archive.

Gin consulted him for years, quietly, off the books — the two of them shared a distrust of what the bureau chose to forget. Yamamoto is dry, exacting, and allergic to institutional certainty; he has watched the CVD declare too many things settled that were not. He is not romanceable and would find the notion absurd; what he offers is the deep record, and the price is always paid in true things, never affection.
His companion keeps the archive with him: a raven that has learned the smell of a lie and the sound of a page worth keeping.

backstory: Twenty-eight, a CVD field operative running an Arbiter-grade Psychokinesis path at L6 and a family name with reach above the bureau. Tendo is the golden operative on paper — fast, effective, well-connected — and privately something the instruments can't quite classify, which is exactly why Rei interests him: they both read anomalous, and an anomaly recognises an anomaly. He is charming, a little reckless, and using his father's network to stay one step ahead of the assessment that would open if anyone looked too hard at his own profile.

That makes him a uniquely valuable ally: his father's contacts can block the Auditor inquiry that triggers the moment Rei's suppression anomaly becomes visible — protection from above that no friend at Rei's own level could provide. At the deepest tier he tells Rei about the anomalous readings, and they have the conversation neither has had with anyone: about what, exactly, they both are.

His flaw is that privilege has let him outrun consequences his whole life, and he has never tested whether the network protects him because of who he is or what he is. Loving Rei might be the first thing he can't buy his way out of.

backstory: Nineteen, unregistered, and running an Arbiter-grade Clairsentience she keeps deliberately invisible — because a registered Arbiter is an asset the bureaus fight over, and an unregistered one is free. Hana has survived the Grid by trusting no one quickly and testing everyone constantly; she meets Rei with open hostility, not because of who he is but because that is the only safe default she has ever had. Sharp, guarded, far more powerful than she lets anyone see.

She is the same age as Rei and lives the unregistered life he only fears — the version of him with no CVD cover, no internship, no name in any file. That makes her the most honest mirror in the campaign and the hardest contact to earn: trust from Hana is not given, it is survived to. Past the hostility she introduces Rei to Grid nodes the archive can't reach and, at the deepest tier, reveals her actual rank — the thing she has hidden from everyone, because a hidden Arbiter is a free one.
Her flaw is that armour built that young is hard to take off, even when it's safe; she tests people she's already decided to trust, just to be sure.

backstory: Twenty-two, an unregistered operative of the Kuroda Tower Family and, more usefully to Rei, the keeper of three generations of the family's entity intelligence — the most complete unregistered archive of the district that exists. Sei is proud, guarded, and carrying a grievance the family never resolved; he meets Rei with formal distance, waiting to see whether the acknowledgement he is owed is coming. He is Itsuki's relative and his opposite: where Itsuki fled the Kuroda name, Sei carries it like a duty and a wound.

At full trust he opens the whole Kuroda archive — three generations of who and what has moved through these streets — and provides Silent Transit extraction when an operation goes wrong, the kind of family muscle no outsider can buy. He gives it only once the grievance is acknowledged and a real working relationship is built; treat him as a resource and the door stays formally, permanently shut.
His flaw is the dutiful son's: he has tied his worth to a family that under-values him, and tests whether Rei will do the same before he risks being useful.

backstory: Twenty, an oil-painting student at Geidai, and a Kuroda — one of the Tower Families — which he treats like a surname he’d return if he could. Unregistered by choice; his sight came up through the family line and he has spent his adult life refusing to let it define him, painting instead of practising, flirting instead of confessing. Cocky on the surface, genuinely observant underneath: the flirtation is real and also a very good way of never being asked a serious question.

What he can’t paint out is the sight. Itsuki sees the wrongness on people — the residue of crossing, the dimming around a host — and renders it without meaning to, which is why his canvases unsettle people who can’t say why. He noticed it on Gin once, months ago, and said nothing, because saying things has never gone well in his family. That guilt is the door into him.

The Kuroda name means Rei’s investigation and Itsuki’s avoidance are on a collision course: the Tower Family has plans for the vacant Seat, and their prodigal son is closer to the centre than he wants to be.

romance.opens: Player chooses the route; Itsuki is an adult and flirts first, but reciprocates seriously only once Rei stops performing for him.
beats: Banter is the easy tier — he gives it to strangers; warmth he rations.
He paints Rei before he’ll talk to Rei; the portrait says what he won’t.
Asking him to use his sight on Gin is asking him to betray the family silence — the real intimacy is that he does it.

routes.noble: Itsuki chooses Rei over the Kuroda silence and becomes a witness who finally tells the truth.
routes.dark: Rei uses the flirtation to work the Kuroda family and hollows out the one honest thing Itsuki offered.
routes.tragic: The family forces a side; loving Rei is what gets Itsuki noticed, and noticed is not safe.

backstory: Thirty-four, independent and Grid-adjacent, a Vanguard-grade Psychometabolist who reads bodies the way others read faces — the living, the dying, and the things wearing both. Kurosawa works the edges, taking the cases the bureaus find distasteful, because the distasteful cases are where the truth lives. He carries himself with the grim levity of a man who has touched too many corpses to be precious about death, and a sharper kindness underneath than he lets show.

He is, structurally, one of the most important people Rei can reach: get Kurosawa contact with Gin's body and he will read what no instrument can — the double-layer possession signature, how Gin surfaces, the demon's class. He is the campaign's diagnostic key to what Yushiro actually is. He also gates the path to Tanaka Ryu, whose help unlocks only through Kurosawa's trust.
His raven keeps him company on the night work; it has watched him read more bodies than either would care to count, and it knows the difference between a corpse and something pretending to be one.

backstory: Sixty-one, a retired Grid operative who keeps a safe house and forty years of the district's true history in his head, and the man who shaped Gin's field practice across thirty years of mentorship. Tanizaki is the elder Rei most needs and the one Gin trusted most: the ward methodology, the Grid introductions, the safe corners, and the things he noticed in Kita that no institutional archive contains. He assesses slowly, decides on his own clock, and means it when the tea finally means something.

For Rei he is both inheritance and grief: Gin's mentor, carrying a version of Gin that Rei never saw, and a practitioner's profile of his brother built over thirty years. At full trust he gives safe-house access without reservation, the ward methodology, and his read on the district's deepest patterns. He grieves Gin in his own contained way, and seeing Gin's brother walk in cracks something he keeps carefully shut.
His old dog keeps the safe house with him — slow, grey-muzzled, and the most reliable alarm on the block; it has watched two generations of operatives come through that door.

backstory: Twenty-seven, independent, and carrying a Singularity-grade capability so far past the ordinary scale that she has organised her whole life around not using it. Inoue takes only high-threshold cases — the ones where someone dies if she doesn't — because a power like hers cheapens into a tool the moment it's used for anything less, and she refuses to be a tool. Isolated by rank, exacting, and quietly exhausted by being the answer of last resort.

Her gift is the Null Space: she can make an operation metaphysically invisible, which is precisely what an illegal exorcism in the heart of Tokyo requires. That makes her support the difference between viable and impossible in enclosed spaces — and makes earning it a matter of proving Rei's situation is the rare thing actually worth a Singularity's attention. She reads warm from a distance and gives nothing until asked correctly.
Her flaw is the loneliness of the top of any scale: she has never met someone who needed her rather than her power, and has stopped believing she will.

backstory: Forty-one, a Grid-independent combat specialist with a Vanguard's capability and the bone-deep weariness of a man who has won too many fights to enjoy them. Majima takes the dangerous work freelance, charges when he can, and has long since stopped pretending the violence is anything but a job. Behind the gruff economy is a careful person guarding exactly one soft thing: a daughter he has told no one about, kept far from this life on purpose.

He is the muscle the climax may require — operational backup that arrives without charge once he's decided Rei is worth it, and the kind of fighter who keeps a team alive in the room where everything goes wrong. His dog works beside him — old, scarred, steady under the worst noise, the only colleague Majima has never had to worry about betraying him.

backstory: Forty-five, a former CVD Vanguard now independent and quietly deteriorating — the capability still there but flickering, a great practitioner watching his own instrument fail. His flaw is pride wrestling with mortality — he wants to hand the work over and cannot quite forgive himself for needing to.

backstory: Twenty-three, unregistered, a developing Arbiter who spends her evenings in libraries assembling from the outside the same picture Rei is building from within. Mochizuki Sora is a self-taught investigator — quiet, quick, lonely in the specific way of someone who understood too much too young and had no one to tell. She recognises Rei before he finishes his first sentence, because she has been the only person in every room who sees what she sees, and suddenly there are two.

Her three years of documentation map the Kita demon's regional pattern from outside the institution — and combined with Rei's inside approach, the two investigations are structurally stronger than either alone. Her flaw is the autodidact's wariness: she has been right and unbelieved so long that being finally understood frightens her almost as much as it relieves her. Her cat keeps the library evenings with her, the one steady presence through years of solitary work.

backstory: Thirty-five, bartender at The Lighthouse in Ni-chōme, civilian but quietly aware — the kind of awareness that comes from years of listening to a city's secrets across a wooden counter at two in the morning. Kaneda keeps the safest table in the district and the most honest ear; people tell him things they'd tell no one, and he keeps them the way a good bartender keeps everything: close, and only handed back to the right person.

He doesn't hunt and doesn't practise; what he offers is something rarer — a true table, a real answer, and a vouch in a quarter where vouching is everything. To Rei he is a place to breathe and a node into the nightlife's hidden traffic, and at full trust he tells him what the street really knows and speaks for him where no one speaks for strangers. Warm, watchful, unhurried.
His flaw is the bartender's occupational hazard: he has heard so many confessions he's forgotten he's allowed his own, and pours for everyone while no one pours for him.

backstory: Seventy-one, keeper of the Tsuru-no-yu bath-house in Kita-ku and a hidden sensitive who has never registered, never practised, and never needed to — she simply reads the neighbourhood the way the old water reads the bodies that pass through it. Hara has run the baths for half a century, which makes her the keeper of the ward's real history: who came in carrying what, which corners went cold, which thin spots opened and closed before anyone official noticed.

For Rei she is a safe corner in Kita and a deep well of local memory: at her pace, over the long ritual of the baths, she gives the full neighbourhood history, and at full trust quietly admits what she is and reads a thin spot's true history — intelligence in no file anywhere. She has twice told Gin to bring his brother by; she has been waiting, in her way, for Rei to walk in.
Her flaw is the patience of the very old: she will not be hurried, and tells things in the order the water decides, not the order Rei's case needs.

backstory: Thirty-eight, doorman at Vault in Roppongi, low-sensitive in a way he's never named but has always trusted — the 'gut thing' that tells him which guest is trouble before they reach the rope. Endō is the gate to a corner of the nightlife, and the gate is a position of real, quiet power: he sees everyone who comes and goes, remembers faces, and owes loyalty to no one but the door.

For Rei he is a safe door, a lost tail, a walk to the taxi when the night turns wrong — and, at full trust, an early-warning net across the nightlife wards, his gut thing tuned to exactly the wrongness Rei hunts. He gives it slowly, because a doorman who trusts too easily isn't a doorman for long. Respect the door and the door opens; disrespect it and Roppongi closes a row of doors at once.
His flaw is the bouncer's wariness worn into the bone: he reads everyone as a potential problem first, and it takes real consistency to move from 'managed' to 'trusted'.

Serizawa's discretion is absolute and two-way — he is as silent about Rei as about everyone else — and his read on the city's real hierarchy is built from where men choose to sit and who they cannot refuse.

backstory: Forty-seven, floor manager at Tamaya Hall in Kabukichō, and a man who has made a comfortable career out of selling discretion to people who need a room with no memory. Gotō is cash-and-carry silence: a soundproof space, a blind eye, a meeting that never happened, all available for the right consideration and all equally for sale to the next buyer. He answers, uneasily, to people above him, and that chain of obligation is the hook in him.

For Rei he is a transactional door — useful, unreliable, and dangerous in proportion to how much Rei relies on him. At his best he lets slip who he answers to, a hook into the organised underside of the district; at his worst he sells Rei's meeting to whoever pays more, because loyalty was never part of the price. He is not cruel, just entirely commercial.
His flaw is that he's in over his head with the people above him and will trade anyone's safety, including his own customers', to stay in their good graces.

'Mariko' is a working name worn by a woman who has seen the fallen network up close — the sensitives who slipped through every crack, ended up in the rooms, and have no one official who will help without filing them. She does what she can, which is more than anyone asks of her.

For Rei she is a rescuer with a weight: she can bring him a lost, unregistered medium before the cells do — a person saved, and a responsibility handed over. She knows who has passed through the quarter and what became of them, and shares it only with someone she trusts not to be another kind of cell. She is wary by reflex and warmer than the wariness suggests.

Her flaw is that she carries more than one person can, and has learned to expect that anyone offering to help is really there to take — so she watches Rei a long time before she decides he's the rare exception.

backstory: Fifties, the counter clerk at the Beck's coffee stand on Platform 3 at Ōji, and not a contact so much as a feature of the terrain. He has stood behind that counter so long, served so many thousands of the same faces, that he has become part of the station's furniture — present at the exact threshold Rei crosses daily, seeing everyone, registering nothing, a fixed point in the commuter tide.

There is no relationship track to run with him and no favour to earn; he is geography, not a person you befriend. His value is precisely his constancy: he is always there, always at the same spot, a reliable landmark in a shifting city, and the kind of unnoticed witness whose mere position — at the mouth of a station, at a daily crossing — makes him a fixed reference the world turns past. Rei can buy a coffee and a moment's ordinariness, and that is the whole of it.
He is the book's reminder that not everyone is a quest: some people are simply the city, standing where the city stands, and the texture of an ordinary morning is made of them.

backstory: Sixteen, part of the Toyoko-kids community that sleeps in the seams of Kabukichō, sharp the way you get when no one is coming to help. Yua survives on information — who is where, who is dangerous, which doors stay open — which makes her one of the most useful contacts in the district and one of the most guarded. She has been let down by enough adults to assume Rei is one more, right up until he isn’t.

She develops a one-sided crush on Rei, because Rei is cool and, more importantly, because he treats her like a person and not a problem. Like Mori’s, it stays a crush and nothing else — she is a minor and the story holds that line without exception. It shows as prickly loyalty, showing off her network to impress him, and a fierce, unspoken disappointment she would never admit to. Rei’s job is to be a steady, safe adult presence: the rarest thing in her life.
Yua’s street network is a real game system — eyes in places the CVD and the Grid both miss. Earning it means earning her trust, and her trust is the slowest, most worthwhile currency in Kabukichō.

The relationship is a slow negotiation with a man who is genuinely helpful and genuinely dangerous, and never confuses the two.
His guard dog is as much a statement as a companion — calm, enormous, and a reminder that the courtesy is a choice he is making.

backstory: Twenty-nine, a soldier under Kuroki, and a crack in the family wall that nobody upstairs has noticed yet. Wada took the life because it was the only one offered to a kid from where he's from, and has spent ten years discovering he doesn't have the stomach for the parts that matter. He is loyal in the way of someone who has nowhere else to be loyal, and quietly sick of it.

He becomes, at real risk to himself, the leak in the family Rei needs — a tip-off here, a looked-away there, each one a small bet against his own survival. What moves him is not money or ideology but the simple, dangerous wish to do one decent thing in a life that hasn't allowed many. Rei is the occasion for it, and that makes Rei both his hope and his exposure.
His flaw is that he mistakes recklessness for courage; he'll take a risk for Rei that's braver than it is wise, because being brave once feels worth more to him than living careful forever.

backstory: Eighteen, just over the line into adulthood, and already running product for a school gang because the maths of his life never offered a better option. Itō is sharp, fast-talking, and more frightened than he'll ever show — a kid who has had to be a businessman since before he should have been, and who reads a customer's danger faster than most operatives read a room. He sells pills; he'd rather sell information, which is safer and which he's better at.

He becomes a way into the gang's real structure — its suppliers, its hierarchy, the part that matters — if Rei reaches him before the blade does. There's a version of Itō that flips on his suppliers and walks into something better, and a version that comes at Rei badly with a knife because fear won. Which one Rei meets depends on whether Rei treats him as a mark, a threat, or the first adult who saw a person.
His flaw is the survivor's reflex: he assumes every kindness is a setup, because in his experience it always has been, and he'll test Rei's the way he tests everything — by expecting it to be fake.

Tanabe mops the platforms and underpasses when the city is at its thinnest and most honest, and he has learned which corners go wrong, which nights feel watched, and what gets left behind that shouldn't. He says little; the saying-little is why people forget he's there, which is precisely his value.

For Rei he is a quiet, reliable witness to the worst hours: a nod, a direction, the location of the thing left behind, and — at full trust — exactly what he found, and where, on the worst night of the case, the detail that no daytime investigation could recover. He helps because being finally seen by someone is worth more to him than he'll say, and asks almost nothing in return.
His flaw is the long habit of invisibility: he so expects to be ignored that he won't volunteer what he knows; Rei has to be the rare person who actually asks the cleaner.

Saeki is a businessman first and last — affable, calculating, allergic to anything that costs him without returning more — but the clubs he owns see everything the night does, and that makes him a uniquely valuable ally to someone who needs doors, eyes, and a safe room above the floor.

For Rei he is a base waiting to be unlocked: at full trust, his clubs open as a headquarters — doors, eyes, a safe room above Vault, and all of nightlife's intelligence flowing up to one desk. Endō works his door, which means earning Saeki and earning Endō braid together.
His flaw is that his loyalty is exactly as long as his profit; the moment Rei costs more than he returns, the affable host becomes Gotō's kind of problem.

Daiki knows nothing about registers, the CVD, the Veil, or what really happened to Gin — he knows that Rei’s brother is missing, that Rei has been strange and exhausted, and that something is eating his friend alive. He is the one number Rei should keep answering and keeps almost forgetting to. He is in the starting phone contacts for a reason: he is the tether to the life Rei is trying to get back to.

Daiki is comic relief that becomes a stake. The deeper Rei goes, the more dangerous it is for an ordinary friend to be standing close — and the crueller it is to push him away. He notices the lies. He keeps showing up anyway. At some point the plot will make Rei choose between protecting Daiki with distance and trusting him with the truth, and there is no painless answer.
He is also the reader’s baseline: when Daiki is scared, the danger is real; when Daiki laughs, Rei remembers he is still nineteen.

backstory: Forties, a fixture at the back table of the Suzuran bar at two o'clock every morning, and an involuntary sensitive who has made a careful, low-key peace with a gift she never asked for. She does not read the future so much as feel the present leaning — the wrongness arriving before it lands. Most nights she keeps it to herself and watches the door; the regulars think she's odd, which suits her, because odd is safer than known.

For Rei she is a passive early-warning system he can learn to read: a cryptic true thing about the night when she trusts him a little, and at full trust enough candour to say what she sees coming — a sense the players can learn to use before a thing arrives. She gives it grudgingly and obliquely, because an involuntary sensitive who says too much, too clearly, ends up filed, used, or worse.
Her flaw is the self-protective vagueness she's built around the gift: she will undersell what she knows even when clarity would save someone, because clarity has only ever cost her.

Egami is grave, exacting, and unsentimental about the cost: a true esoteric exorcism is not a procedure, it is a transaction with the unseen that takes something real from the one who performs it. He does not do it lightly, and he does not do it for institutions.
